title: They also reject the common Roman view of the easier precepts, and the Spanish view reported by Vázquez
source_text: XLIX. Praeterea manifestum est ex iis quae diximus, communi Protestantium calculo improbari, quod longe maxima pars Scholae Romanae docet, nimirum praecepta legis moralis faciliora, absque Christi gratia, ab homine corrupto sic observari posse, ut actus sit vere bonus & in eo peccatum vitetur, quanquam ad salutem aeternam non prosit: ac multo magis eorum sententiam qui in ista Schola tenuerunt, totam Naturae legem posse citra gratiam impleri ab homine lapso, aut si non ejus omnia praecepta collective, saltem singula disjunctive, ut in Hispania multi, teste Gabriele Vasquez, sub finem superioris saeculi sentiebant.
pass_a_gloss: XLIX. Moreover it is manifest from those things which we have said, that by the common vote of the Protestants is disapproved, what by far the greatest part of the Roman School teaches, namely that the easier precepts of the moral law, without Christ's grace, can by corrupt man be so observed, that the act be truly good and in it sin be avoided, although to eternal salvation it profit not: and much more the opinion of those who in that School have held, that the whole law of Nature can without grace be fulfilled by fallen man, or if not all its precepts collectively, at least each one disjunctively, as in Spain many, by witness of Gabriel Vázquez, towards the end of the former century thought.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLIX. It is also clear from what we have said that the Protestants by common vote reject what by far the largest part of the Roman School teaches: that the easier precepts of the moral law can be kept by corrupt man without the grace of Christ in such a way that the act is truly good and sin is avoided in it, even though it does nothing for eternal salvation.

Much more do they reject the view of those in that School who held that fallen man can fulfil the whole law of nature without grace, or, if not all its precepts together, at least each one taken singly. Many in Spain thought so toward the end of the last century, as Gabriel Vázquez testifies.
